title: Three exit interviews
text:
In eleven months, seven people left the customer service team. Staff turnover reached 58%, the highest in the company.

The standard explanation was salary. The team was paid slightly below market, and everyone repeated this until it sounded like a fact.

Then the HR manager read three exit interviews in the same week. All three mentioned money once, briefly. All three spent longer describing the same thing: shifts published on Friday evening for the week starting Monday.

People couldn't book a dentist. They couldn't promise to collect a child. One woman said she had cancelled the same course three times.

The fix cost nothing. Shifts moved to a three-week rolling schedule, published on the first of each month. Two people were given fixed patterns because of childcare.

Turnover in the following year was 12%.

The HR manager made one more change afterwards, and she says it mattered more than the schedule. Exit interviews are now read by the department head, not filed. Her reason was simple: the answers had been sitting in a folder for two years.

questions.q: What did everyone assume the problem was?
What did the exit interviews actually reveal?
options: Shifts were published too late to plan a life
The office was too far away

questions.q: What happened to staff turnover after the change?
What second change did the HR manager make?
options: Exit interviews are now read by the department head

title: The candidate who asked back
text:
The vacancy was for an office coordinator. Forty applications arrived, and the shortlist had five names.

Four of the five interviews followed the same pattern. Good answers, prepared examples, and then, at the end, no questions. Or one polite question about the start date.

The fifth candidate, Nadia, asked three. What does success look like in this role after six months? What does the person doing it now find most frustrating? And who would she work with most closely?

The hiring manager admitted afterwards that she couldn't answer the second question properly, which told her something about the job description.

Nadia got the offer letter on Thursday. She accepted on Monday, after asking one more question about the probation period and the training budget.

Six months later she had reorganised the filing system and reduced the enrolment workflow from nine steps to five.

At the next recruitment round, the manager added something to her notes. Candidates who ask about frustration are usually the ones who fix things.

questions.q: What made Nadia different from the other candidates?
options: She asked serious questions at the end

questions.q: What did the manager realise during the interview?
options: She couldn't answer a question about the role's frustrations

questions.q: What did Nadia ask about before accepting?
options: The probation period and training budget

questions.q: What did the manager add to her notes?
options: Candidates who ask about frustration often fix things
